quiz.explain: Relax edges of each vertex once in topological order.

lessons.title: All-Pairs Shortest Paths: Floyd-Warshall and Johnson
lessons.content:
Imagine the back page of an old Bangladesh road atlas: a big table showing the distance between every pair of district towns, Dhaka to Chattogram, Rajshahi to Khulna, Sylhet to Barishal, all of them. Someone had to compute the shortest road distance for every pair. Running a single-source algorithm from every town is one way. In this lesson we learn a neat DP that fills the whole table at once, the Floyd-Warshall algorithm, along with path reconstruction, transitive closure and Johnson's idea for sparse graphs.

The all-pairs problem: Given a directed weighted graph with V vertices, compute delta(i, j), the shortest path weight, for every ordered pair (i, j). The output is a V by V matrix. Negative edges are allowed, but negative cycles are not, because then shortest paths are not defined. We usually store the graph as an adjacency matrix W, with W[i][i] = 0, W[i][j] = edge weight, or infinity if there is no edge.

Option 1, repeat single-source: Run Dijkstra from each vertex: V times O(E log V), so O(VE log V). Good for sparse graphs with non-negative weights. Run Bellman-Ford from each vertex: V times O(VE), which is O(V^2 E), and up to O(V^4) for dense graphs. Too slow. Floyd-Warshall gives O(V^3) with a tiny constant and allows negative edges.

Another DP, by number of edges: CLRS also shows a slower DP where L_m[i][j] is the shortest path from i to j using at most m edges. Then L_m[i][j] = min over k of L_(m-1)[i][k] + W[k][j]. This looks exactly like matrix multiplication with + replaced by min and times replaced by +. Computing L_(V-1) step by step costs O(V^4), and with repeated squaring, the same trick as fast exponentiation in lesson 8, it drops to O(V^3 log V). Floyd-Warshall's smarter choice of subproblem, by allowed intermediate vertices instead of by number of edges, removes the log factor entirely.

The key idea, intermediate vertices: Number the vertices 1 to V. For a path from i to j, its intermediate vertices are all vertices on it except i and j. Define d_k[i][j] = the weight of the shortest path from i to j whose intermediate vertices all belong to the set {1, 2, ..., k}. With k = 0, no intermediate vertices are allowed, so d_0[i][j] = W[i][j]. With k = V, any vertex may be used, so d_V[i][j] = delta(i, j).

The recurrence: Consider the shortest path from i to j using only intermediate vertices from {1, ..., k}. Either it does not use vertex k, so its weight is d_(k-1)[i][j], or it does use k exactly once (no negative cycles, so no reason to repeat it), splitting into i to k and k to j, both using only {1, ..., k-1}. So d_k[i][j] = min(d_(k-1)[i][j], d_(k-1)[i][k] + d_(k-1)[k][j]). That is the entire algorithm.

The code: for k from 1 to V: for i from 1 to V: for j from 1 to V: if d[i][k] + d[k][j] < d[i][j]: d[i][j] = d[i][k] + d[k][j]. Three nested loops, with k outermost. It is safe to update a single matrix in place, because during round k, row k and column k do not change: d[i][k] + d[k][k] = d[i][k] since d[k][k] = 0. Time Theta(V^3), space Theta(V^2).

Why k must be the outer loop: The recurrence builds on 'allowed intermediate sets' that grow one vertex at a time. If you put i or j outermost, you would use values that do not yet include the right intermediate vertices and get wrong answers. This is the most famous Floyd-Warshall bug, and exams ask about it directly.

Worked example, the graph: Four vertices. Edges: 1 to 2 weight 3, 1 to 4 weight 7, 2 to 1 weight 8, 2 to 3 weight 2, 3 to 1 weight 5, 3 to 4 weight 1, 4 to 1 weight 2. Initial matrix rows: row 1 = [0, 3, inf, 7], row 2 = [8, 0, 2, inf], row 3 = [5, inf, 0, 1], row 4 = [2, inf, inf, 0].

Worked example, k = 1 and k = 2: Allow vertex 1 as an intermediate. New paths through 1: 2 to 4 via 1 = 8 + 7 = 15; 3 to 2 via 1 = 5 + 3 = 8; 4 to 2 via 1 = 2 + 3 = 5. Rows: [0, 3, inf, 7], [8, 0, 2, 15], [5, 8, 0, 1], [2, 5, inf, 0]. Allow vertex 2: 1 to 3 via 2 = 3 + 2 = 5; 4 to 3 via 2 = 5 + 2 = 7. Rows: [0, 3, 5, 7], [8, 0, 2, 15], [5, 8, 0, 1], [2, 5, 7, 0].

Worked example, k = 3 and k = 4: Allow vertex 3: 1 to 4 via 3 = 5 + 1 = 6, better than 7; 2 to 1 via 3 = 2 + 5 = 7, better than 8; 2 to 4 via 3 = 2 + 1 = 3, better than 15. Allow vertex 4: 2 to 1 via 4 = 3 + 2 = 5; 3 to 1 via 4 = 1 + 2 = 3; 3 to 2 via 4 = 1 + 5 = 6. Final rows: [0, 3, 5, 6], [5, 0, 2, 3], [3, 6, 0, 1], [2, 5, 7, 0]. For example, the shortest path from 2 to 1 is 5, along 2, 3, 4, 1.

Path reconstruction: Keep a second matrix next[i][j], the first step on a shortest path from i to j. Initialise next[i][j] = j when there is an edge. Whenever d[i][j] is improved through k, set next[i][j] = next[i][k]. To print the path from i to j: start at i, repeatedly move to next[current][j] until you reach j. CLRS uses a predecessor matrix pi[i][j] instead, the vertex before j; either style works. For 2 to 1 in our example: next[2][1] = 3, next[3][1] = 4, next[4][1] = 1, giving 2, 3, 4, 1.

Detecting negative cycles: Floyd-Warshall can also detect negative cycles. After the algorithm, if any diagonal entry d[i][i] is negative, then vertex i lies on a negative cycle, because a path from i back to itself has negative weight. This is a quick check to add at the end.

Transitive closure: Sometimes we do not need distances, only reachability: can i reach j at all? The transitive closure is a Boolean matrix T with T[i][j] = 1 if there is a path from i to j. Warshall's algorithm uses the same loops with OR and AND: T[i][j] = T[i][j] or (T[i][k] and T[k][j]). Time Theta(V^3) but with simple bit operations, very fast in practice. Bit-packing rows makes it even faster.

Transitive closure example: Course prerequisites again: Programming to Data Structures, Data Structures to Algorithms, Algorithms to Compiler. The closure tells us Programming is an indirect prerequisite of Compiler, so a student who failed Programming cannot take Compiler. One closure table answers every 'is X needed before Y?' question instantly.

Johnson's algorithm, the idea: For sparse graphs with negative edges, Johnson's algorithm beats Floyd-Warshall. Step 1, add a new vertex q with zero-weight edges to every vertex, and run Bellman-Ford from q to get h(v) = delta(q, v); this also detects negative cycles. Step 2, reweight every edge: w'(u, v) = w(u, v) + h(u) - h(v). These new weights are all non-negative. Step 3, run Dijkstra from every vertex with w'. Step 4, convert back: delta(u, v) = delta'(u, v) - h(u) + h(v).

Why reweighting works: For any path from u to v, the new weight equals the old weight plus h(u) - h(v), because the h terms of the middle vertices cancel like a telescope. So every path between the same two vertices shifts by the same amount, and the shortest path stays the shortest. Non-negativity comes from the triangle inequality h(v) <= h(u) + w(u, v). The total time is O(VE log V) with binary heaps, better than V^3 when E is much smaller than V^2.

Which algorithm to choose: Dense graph, any weights without negative cycles: Floyd-Warshall, O(V^3), simplest code. Sparse graph, non-negative weights: Dijkstra from every vertex. Sparse graph with negative weights: Johnson. Only reachability: Warshall's transitive closure or a BFS/DFS from every vertex, O(V(V + E)).

Real life example 1, a bus company's fare and distance chart: A long-route bus company serving 30 towns wants a chart of the shortest road distance between every pair of towns, printed at its counters. With only 30 towns, Floyd-Warshall needs 27,000 simple steps, nothing for a computer. Path reconstruction also tells the company which towns a trip passes through, useful for planning stops.

Real life example 2, social networks and reachability: On a messaging app, a school group might want to know who can forward messages to whom through chains of contacts. Transitive closure answers this for small groups. For network routers, link-state protocols like OSPF compute shortest paths to all destinations, usually by running Dijkstra from each router, which is the 'repeat single-source' approach.

Common mistakes: First, putting the k loop inside instead of outside. Second, forgetting that d[i][i] starts at 0. Third, adding infinity plus a number and getting overflow in code; check for infinity first. Fourth, using Floyd-Warshall on a graph with negative cycles without checking the diagonal. Fifth, in Johnson, forgetting to convert distances back after Dijkstra.

What exams ask: 'Apply Floyd-Warshall to this 4-vertex graph and show the matrix after each k.' 'Write the recurrence and explain why k must be the outermost loop.' 'Reconstruct the path from i to j using the predecessor matrix.' 'Compute the transitive closure.' 'Explain the reweighting in Johnson's algorithm and why it preserves shortest paths.' Draw each matrix clearly; examiners check D1, D2, D3 and D4 separately.

A tip for hand computation: In round k, only row k and column k matter. For each cell (i, j), add the entry in column k of row i to the entry in row k of column j, and compare with the current cell. Cross out row k and column k on your page, since they do not change, and cells where either needed value is infinity can be skipped instantly. Also, cells in row k and column k themselves never change in round k, so you only need to check (V - 1) times (V - 1) cells, which for a 4-vertex graph means 9 cells per round instead of 16.

Recap: All-pairs shortest paths fills a V by V matrix. Floyd-Warshall uses d_k[i][j] = min(d_(k-1)[i][j], d_(k-1)[i][k] + d_(k-1)[k][j]) with k as the outer loop, Theta(V^3) time, Theta(V^2) space, negative edges allowed. A predecessor or next matrix rebuilds paths; a negative diagonal reveals a negative cycle. Warshall's version computes transitive closure. Johnson reweights with Bellman-Ford and runs Dijkstra from every vertex for sparse graphs. Next: maximum flow.
key_points: All-pairs shortest paths computes a V x V distance matrix; negative edges allowed, negative cycles not.
Floyd-Warshall: d_k[i][j] = min(d_(k-1)[i][j], d_(k-1)[i][k] + d_(k-1)[k][j]).
k must be the outermost loop; Theta(V^3) time, Theta(V^2) space, in-place update is safe.
A next or predecessor matrix rebuilds paths; negative d[i][i] reveals a negative cycle.
Warshall's transitive closure: T[i][j] = T[i][j] or (T[i][k] and T[k][j]).
Johnson: Bellman-Ford from a new vertex gives h, reweight w' = w + h(u) - h(v) >= 0, then Dijkstra from every vertex; O(VE log V).
Dense graphs: Floyd-Warshall; sparse non-negative: repeated Dijkstra; sparse with negatives: Johnson.
lessons.tip: In Floyd-Warshall exam questions, box row k and column k of each matrix before computing. It halves the work and makes mistakes easy to spot.
lessons.task: Choose 4 nearby places and write a 4 x 4 table of direct travel minutes (infinity where there is no direct road). Run Floyd-Warshall on paper, writing the matrix after each k, and check one answer by finding the route yourself.

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of Floyd-Warshall?
quiz.explain: Three nested loops over V vertices.

quiz.q: Which loop must be outermost in Floyd-Warshall?
quiz.explain: The recurrence grows the allowed intermediate set one vertex at a time.

quiz.q: After Floyd-Warshall, a negative value d[i][i] means
options: There is no path from i
Vertex i is on a negative cycle
quiz.explain: A path from i back to i with negative weight is a negative cycle.

quiz.q: In the example graph, what is the shortest distance from 2 to 1?
quiz.explain: Path 2, 3, 4, 1 with weight 2 + 1 + 2 = 5.

quiz.q: Johnson's algorithm reweights edges with w'(u,v) = w(u,v) + h(u) - h(v). Why does this keep shortest paths?
options: All paths between the same pair shift by h(u) - h(v)
quiz.explain: Middle h terms cancel, so every u-to-v path changes by the same constant.

lessons.title: Maximum Flow: Ford-Fulkerson, Edmonds-Karp, Min Cut, Matching
lessons.content:
Imagine WASA pumping water from a treatment plant to a neighbourhood through a network of pipes. Each pipe can carry at most a certain number of litres per second, and water cannot pile up at the joints: whatever flows in must flow out. How much water per second can reach the neighbourhood at most? This is the maximum flow problem. The same question appears for traffic on roads, data in networks and goods on supply chains. In this lesson we learn flow networks, residual graphs, augmenting paths, Ford-Fulkerson, Edmonds-Karp, the max-flow min-cut theorem and bipartite matching.

Flow networks: A flow network is a directed graph G = (V, E) with a source s, a sink t and a non-negative capacity c(u, v) on each edge. A flow assigns a value f(u, v) to each edge with two rules. Capacity constraint: 0 <= f(u, v) <= c(u, v). Flow conservation: for every vertex other than s and t, total flow in equals total flow out. The value of the flow, |f|, is the total flow leaving s, which equals the total flow entering t. The goal is a flow of maximum value.

A tiny example: Vertices s, a, b, t. Edges: s to a capacity 3, s to b capacity 2, a to b capacity 1, a to t capacity 2, b to t capacity 3. One flow: send 2 along s, a, t; 2 along s, b, t; and 1 along s, a, b, t. Check conservation at a: in 3, out 2 + 1 = 3. At b: in 2 + 1 = 3, out 3. Value 5. Can we do better? Everything leaving s is already full, 3 + 2 = 5, so no.

Why greedy path filling fails: A natural idea is to repeatedly find any path from s to t with room left and push as much as possible. But a bad early choice can block the best answer. Example: s to a 1, s to b 1, a to b 1, a to t 1, b to t 1. If the first path is s, a, b, t, we send 1, and now s to a, a to b and b to t are full. No more paths seem to exist, giving 1. But the maximum is 2: s, a, t and s, b, t. We need a way to undo flow, and that is what the residual graph provides.

The residual graph: Given a flow f, the residual capacity of edge (u, v) is c_f(u, v) = c(u, v) - f(u, v), the room left. We also add a reverse edge (v, u) with residual capacity f(u, v), meaning we may cancel up to that much flow. The residual graph G_f contains all edges with positive residual capacity. In the bad example, after sending 1 on s, a, b, t, the residual graph has a reverse edge b to a with capacity 1. Now the path s, b, a, t exists in G_f: it cancels the flow on a to b and redirects it. Total 2.

Augmenting paths: An augmenting path is a simple path from s to t in the residual graph. Its bottleneck is the smallest residual capacity on it. Augmenting means: for each edge on the path, if it is a forward edge, add the bottleneck to its flow; if it is a reverse edge, subtract the bottleneck from the flow of the original edge. The flow value increases by the bottleneck, and the capacity and conservation rules remain true.

The Ford-Fulkerson method: Start with zero flow. While there is an augmenting path p in G_f: augment along p by its bottleneck. When no augmenting path exists, stop; the flow is maximum. It is called a method because it does not say how to pick the path. With integer capacities, each augmentation adds at least 1, so it terminates after at most |f*| augmentations, where f* is a maximum flow. Each search costs O(E), so the time is O(E |f*|).

A weakness of plain Ford-Fulkerson: The bound depends on the flow value, not on the graph size. Classic bad case: s to a and s to b and a to t and b to t with capacity 1,000,000, and a middle edge a to b with capacity 1. If the paths alternate between s, a, b, t and s, b, a, t (using the reverse edge), each augmentation adds only 1, needing two million augmentations instead of two. With irrational capacities, a bad choice can even fail to terminate. So the choice of path matters.

Edmonds-Karp: Choose the augmenting path with the fewest edges, found by BFS in the residual graph. This simple rule guarantees at most O(VE) augmentations, independent of capacities. Each BFS costs O(E), so the total time is O(V E^2). It always terminates, even with real-number capacities. In exams, 'Ford-Fulkerson with BFS' means Edmonds-Karp.

Cuts: An s-t cut (S, T) splits the vertices into S containing s and T containing t. Its capacity c(S, T) is the sum of capacities of edges going from S to T; edges from T back to S do not count. For any flow and any cut, the net flow across the cut equals |f|, so |f| <= c(S, T). In words, no flow can exceed any cut, like water through the narrowest band of pipes.

The max-flow min-cut theorem: The following three statements are equivalent. One, f is a maximum flow. Two, the residual graph G_f has no augmenting path. Three, |f| = c(S, T) for some cut. So the value of the maximum flow equals the capacity of the minimum cut. This theorem proves Ford-Fulkerson correct, and it also gives a way to find a minimum cut: after the algorithm ends, let S be all vertices reachable from s in the residual graph. That (S, V - S) is a minimum cut.

Min cut in the tiny example: After the maximum flow of 5, from s in the residual graph, both s to a and s to b are full, so no vertex is reachable. S = {s}, T = {a, b, t}. Edges from S to T: s to a 3 and s to b 2, total 5. The cut capacity equals the flow value, confirming the theorem. The minimum cut shows the bottleneck: the pipes leaving the plant.

Edmonds-Karp worked example: Network: s to a 10, s to b 5, a to b 15, a to t 5, b to t 10. BFS finds the shortest path s, a, t with bottleneck 5: flow 5. Next BFS: s, b, t, bottleneck 5: flow 10. Next BFS: s, a, b, t, bottleneck min(5, 15, 5) = 5: flow 15. Now b to t is full and a to t is full, so t cannot be reached. Maximum flow 15. Minimum cut: S = {s, a, b}, edges a to t 5 and b to t 10, total 15.

Bipartite matching: A bipartite graph has two sides L and R, with edges only between sides. A matching is a set of edges with no shared vertex. Maximum bipartite matching asks for the largest matching. Example: L = students, R = projects, an edge means the student can do that project; each student gets at most one project and each project at most one student.

Matching as flow: Add a source s with an edge of capacity 1 to every vertex in L, an edge of capacity 1 from every vertex in R to a sink t, and direct every original edge from L to R with capacity 1. Run Ford-Fulkerson. Because capacities are integers, there is an integer maximum flow, where every edge carries 0 or 1. The edges from L to R carrying 1 form a maximum matching, and its size equals the max-flow value. Time O(VE) with plain Ford-Fulkerson, since the flow is at most V. Specialised algorithms like Hopcroft-Karp do it in O(E sqrt(V)).

Matching example: Students Anik, Bushra, Chayan; projects 1, 2, 3. Anik can do 1 or 2, Bushra only 1, Chayan 2 or 3. Augmenting paths: s, Anik, 1, t; then s, Bushra, 1 is blocked, but the residual reverse edge lets s, Bushra, 1, Anik, 2, t move Anik to project 2; then s, Chayan, 3, t. Matching: Anik 2, Bushra 1, Chayan 3, size 3. The reverse edge did the reassignment automatically.

Real life example 1, Eid traffic out of Dhaka: Before Eid, millions travel from Dhaka to the districts. Treat roads, bridges and ferry routes as edges with capacities in vehicles per hour. The maximum flow from Dhaka to the north-west tells planners how many vehicles per hour can leave at best, and the minimum cut shows the real bottlenecks, for example a bridge and a highway section. Increasing capacity anywhere else does not help; only widening the min cut edges does.

Real life example 2, assigning doctors to clinics: A health project wants to assign doctors to rural clinics; each doctor can work only in certain upazilas due to language or travel, and each clinic needs one doctor. Bipartite matching via max flow gives the largest number of clinics that can be staffed. If it is less than the number of clinics, the min cut shows which group of clinics lacks eligible doctors, a useful message for planners.

Common mistakes: First, forgetting reverse edges in the residual graph, which makes the algorithm get stuck below the maximum. Second, counting edges from T to S in the cut capacity. Third, thinking the min cut is just the smallest single edge. Fourth, saying Ford-Fulkerson is always polynomial; with plain DFS it is O(E |f*|), pseudo-polynomial. Fifth, in matching, forgetting capacity 1 on the source and sink edges, which would let a student take two projects.

What exams ask: 'Run Ford-Fulkerson or Edmonds-Karp on this network, show the residual graph after each augmentation, and give the max flow.' 'Find the minimum cut.' 'State and explain the max-flow min-cut theorem.' 'Why are reverse edges needed?' 'Reduce bipartite matching to max flow and solve this instance.' Draw the residual graph neatly with forward and reverse capacities after every step.

A note on newer algorithms: Push-relabel algorithms, such as Goldberg-Tarjan, work differently: they push excess flow locally and relabel heights, reaching O(V^3) or better, and are fast in practice. Research has recently produced almost linear time max flow algorithms, but those are well beyond an undergraduate course. For exams, Ford-Fulkerson and Edmonds-Karp are what you need.

Recap: A flow respects capacities and conservation; its value is the flow out of s. The residual graph has leftover capacities and reverse edges that let us cancel flow. Ford-Fulkerson augments along residual paths until none remain, O(E |f*|) with integer capacities. Edmonds-Karp picks shortest paths by BFS, O(VE^2). Max flow equals min cut, and the vertices reachable from s in the final residual graph give a min cut. Bipartite matching is max flow with unit capacities. Next: backtracking and branch and bound.
key_points: A flow obeys capacity (0 <= f <= c) and conservation (in = out except at s and t); value = flow out of s.
Residual capacity c - f, plus reverse edges with capacity f to cancel flow.
Ford-Fulkerson: augment along residual s-t paths by their bottleneck until none remain; O(E |f*|) for integers.
Edmonds-Karp picks shortest augmenting paths by BFS: O(V E^2), always terminates.
Max-flow min-cut: max flow value = min cut capacity; vertices reachable from s in the final residual graph give a min cut.
Cut capacity counts only edges from S to T.
Bipartite matching = max flow with unit capacities from s to L, L to R, R to t.
lessons.tip: After every augmentation, redraw the residual graph completely, including reverse edges. Updating in your head is where flow questions go wrong.
lessons.task: Draw a small pipe network of 5 or 6 junctions with capacities from your imagination (or roads around your area with lanes as capacities). Find the maximum flow by augmenting paths on paper, then find a cut with the same capacity to prove it is maximum.

quiz.q: Which rule says inflow equals outflow at every vertex except s and t?
quiz.explain: Conservation keeps flow from piling up at joints.

quiz.q: Why does the residual graph contain reverse edges?
options: To allow cancelling flow sent earlier
quiz.explain: Reverse edges let augmenting paths reroute earlier choices.

quiz.q: What is the running time of Edmonds-Karp?
quiz.explain: O(VE) augmentations, each found by an O(E) BFS.

quiz.q: By the max-flow min-cut theorem, the maximum flow value equals
options: The capacity of a minimum s-t cut
quiz.explain: No flow can exceed any cut, and at the maximum some cut is saturated.

quiz.q: In network s-a 10, s-b 5, a-b 15, a-t 5, b-t 10, what is the max flow?
quiz.explain: The cut {a-t, b-t} has capacity 15 and three augmenting paths reach it.

lessons.title: Backtracking and Branch and Bound
lessons.content:
Imagine you are solving a Sudoku in the newspaper. You write a 4 in an empty box, then a 7 in the next, and after a few moves you find that some row needs two 4s. You do not throw the whole paper away; you erase back to the last guess that went wrong and try another number. That is backtracking: build a solution step by step, and the moment it cannot possibly succeed, step back and try the next option. Branch and bound adds one more idea: if a partial solution cannot beat the best answer found so far, cut it off too. Both are smart ways of searching huge spaces of possibilities.

When we need these methods: Some problems, like N-queens, subset sum, graph colouring, 0/1 knapsack with huge capacities or the travelling salesman problem, have no known polynomial algorithm. Many are NP-hard, as lesson 25 will explain. The honest approach is to search through candidates, but cleverly, so that most bad candidates are rejected early, before being fully built.

The state-space tree: Picture every partial solution as a node in a tree. The root is the empty solution. Each child adds one more decision, like placing the next queen or deciding whether to include the next item. Leaves are complete candidates. Brute force visits every node; backtracking does a DFS on this tree but prunes, meaning it refuses to enter a subtree as soon as it knows no valid solution lies there. A node is called promising if it might still lead to a solution, and non-promising otherwise.

The backtracking template: backtrack(partial): if partial is a complete solution: record it; return. For each choice c for the next step: if c is consistent with partial: add c; backtrack(partial); remove c. The 'remove c' step is the undo, the eraser in the Sudoku story. The consistency check is where all the intelligence lives; a good check prunes huge parts of the tree.

N-queens, the problem: Place N queens on an N by N chessboard so that no two attack each other: no two in the same row, column or diagonal. Since each row must contain exactly one queen, we place queens row by row and only choose the column. Two queens at (r1, c1) and (r2, c2) attack each other if c1 = c2 or |r1 - r2| = |c1 - c2|.

N-queens, worked example for N = 4: Row 1, column 1. Row 2: columns 1 and 2 are attacked, try column 3. Row 3: every column is attacked (1 by column, 2 and 4 by diagonals, 3 by column), so backtrack. Row 2, column 4. Row 3: column 2 is safe. Row 4: every column is attacked, backtrack. Row 3 has no other option, row 2 has no more, so backtrack to row 1 and try column 2. Row 2: column 4. Row 3: column 1. Row 4: column 3. Solution: columns (2, 4, 1, 3). The other solution for N = 4 is its mirror (3, 1, 4, 2).

N-queens, how much pruning helps: Brute force over all placements of 8 queens on 64 squares checks over 4 billion arrangements. Even one queen per row gives 8^8, about 16.7 million. Backtracking with the column and diagonal checks visits only a few thousand nodes for N = 8 and finds all 92 solutions. Keeping three Boolean arrays, for columns, for r + c diagonals and for r - c diagonals, makes each safety check O(1).

Subset sum, the problem: Given positive numbers and a target T, find a subset that adds up to exactly T. Example: {3, 5, 6, 7} and T = 15. The state-space tree is binary: at level i, decide include or exclude the i-th number. There are 2^n leaves.

Subset sum, pruning rules: Sort the numbers in increasing order. At a node with current sum s and remaining numbers with total r: prune if s > T, since adding more only increases the sum; prune if s + r < T, since even taking everything left is not enough; and, because the list is sorted, prune if s plus the next number already exceeds T, as every later number is even bigger. For {3, 5, 6, 7}, T = 15: include 3 (s = 3), include 5 (s = 8), include 6 (s = 14, now 14 + 7 > 15, so exclude 7, s stays 14 < 15, dead end), back, exclude 6, include 7 (s = 15). Found {3, 5, 7}.

Graph colouring, the problem: Colour the vertices of a graph with at most m colours so that adjacent vertices get different colours. The decision version, 'can it be done with m colours?', is NP-complete for m >= 3. Backtracking: colour vertices one by one in a fixed order; for vertex v, try colours 1 to m and accept a colour only if no already-coloured neighbour has it; if no colour works, backtrack to the previous vertex.

Graph colouring example: A map of four districts in a cycle, A next to B, B next to C, C next to D, D next to A, plus A next to C. With m = 3: A = 1, B = 2, C must differ from A and B, so C = 3, D must differ from C and A, so D = 2. Done. With m = 2 the search fails because A, B, C form a triangle. Exam timetables use the same idea: courses are vertices, an edge means a shared student, and colours are time slots.

Branch and bound, the idea: For optimisation problems, we want the best solution, not just any. Branch and bound explores the state-space tree but keeps the best complete solution found so far, called the incumbent. For each node it computes a bound, an optimistic estimate of the best value any solution in its subtree could reach. If the bound is no better than the incumbent, the whole subtree is pruned. Nodes are often explored best-first, using a priority queue ordered by bound, so promising branches are tried early.

0/1 knapsack with branch and bound: Sort items by value per weight. At each node we have decided some items. The upper bound is the current value plus the fractional knapsack value of the remaining items with the remaining capacity, which is optimistic because fractions are allowed. If that bound is not higher than the best complete value found so far, prune the node.

Knapsack bound example: Capacity 50, items (10 kg, 60), (20 kg, 100), (30 kg, 120). Root bound is the fractional answer 240. Branch on item 1: include it, value 60, bound 240; exclude it, bound = 100 + (30/30) 120 = 220. Explore 'include 1'. Include 2: value 160, weight 30, bound 160 + (20/30) 120 = 240. Include 3 is impossible (weight 60 > 50); exclude 3: complete, value 160, incumbent 160. Back to 'include 1, exclude 2': bound 60 + 120 = 180 > 160, explore: include 3, value 180, weight 40, new incumbent 180. Now 'exclude 1' has bound 220 > 180: include 2 and 3, weight 50, value 220. New incumbent 220. Any remaining node with bound <= 220 is pruned. Optimal value 220.

Travelling salesman, the idea: TSP asks for the shortest tour visiting every city exactly once and returning home. For n cities there are (n - 1)!/2 different tours, astronomically many. Branch and bound for TSP builds tours city by city and uses a lower bound on the cost of completing a partial tour, for example the reduced cost matrix method: subtract each row's minimum and each column's minimum; the total subtracted is a lower bound on any tour. Branches whose bound exceeds the best tour found are pruned. It solves moderate instances exactly, though the worst case is still exponential.

Backtracking versus branch and bound: Backtracking is usually for decision or enumeration problems: find one or all solutions that satisfy constraints. It uses DFS and prunes by feasibility. Branch and bound is for optimisation: find the best solution. It prunes by both feasibility and bounds, and often uses best-first or breadth-first order instead of plain DFS. Both remain exponential in the worst case; they win by pruning in practice.

Backtracking versus dynamic programming: DP works when subproblems overlap and can be indexed by small parameters, like capacity W in knapsack. If W is huge but n is small, DP's table is too big, and branch and bound is better. If n is large but W is small, DP wins. Choosing between them is a real engineering decision.

Real life example 1, exam routine at a university: The exam controller must schedule 40 course exams into as few days as possible so no student has two exams on the same day. This is graph colouring. Backtracking with good ordering, colouring courses with the most conflicts first, finds a valid routine quickly for realistic sizes, and tells the controller when the number of days is too small.

Real life example 2, a delivery van route: A courier company in Chattogram has a van that must visit 12 shops and return to the depot. 12 cities give 11!/2, about 20 million tours, too many to list but fine for branch and bound with a good lower bound, which might explore only a tiny fraction. For hundreds of shops, companies switch to approximation and heuristics, as lesson 26 will show.

Common mistakes: First, forgetting to undo the choice after the recursive call returns, so later branches see a dirty state. Second, checking constraints only at the leaves, which throws away the whole benefit of pruning. Third, in branch and bound, using a bound that is not optimistic; an underestimated upper bound for maximisation can prune the true optimum. Fourth, believing backtracking makes NP-hard problems polynomial; it does not, it only makes many instances fast.

What exams ask: 'Draw the state-space tree for 4-queens and show where backtracking occurs.' 'Solve subset sum for {3, 5, 6, 7}, T = 15 with pruning.' 'Explain the m-colouring backtracking algorithm and colour this graph with 3 colours.' 'Solve this 0/1 knapsack instance by branch and bound, showing bounds at each node.' 'Compare backtracking and branch and bound.' Draw the tree, mark pruned nodes with a cross, and write the bound next to each node.

Tips for better pruning: Order choices cleverly, for example most constrained variable first in colouring, or items with highest value per weight first in knapsack. Use cheap, strong checks early. Remember symmetry: in N-queens you only need to try the first queen in the left half of row 1 and mirror the results. Good ordering can turn an impossible search into a quick one.

Recap: Backtracking builds solutions step by step in a state-space tree and abandons any partial solution that cannot be completed. N-queens places one queen per row with O(1) attack checks; subset sum prunes by sum limits; graph colouring tries colours vertex by vertex. Branch and bound adds an optimistic bound and prunes subtrees that cannot beat the incumbent, as in knapsack with the fractional bound and TSP with reduced cost bounds. Next: string matching.
key_points: Backtracking = DFS on the state-space tree that abandons partial solutions that cannot succeed.
Template: choose, check consistency, recurse, undo.
N-queens: one queen per row; attack if same column or |r1 - r2| = |c1 - c2|; 8-queens has 92 solutions.
Subset sum: sort, prune when the sum exceeds T or cannot reach T with the remaining numbers.
Graph colouring: try colours vertex by vertex, rejecting colours used by coloured neighbours.
Branch and bound: keep the incumbent, compute an optimistic bound per node, prune if it cannot beat the incumbent.
Knapsack bound = value + fractional knapsack of the rest; TSP uses reduced cost matrix bounds; worst case stays exponential.
lessons.tip: When drawing a state-space tree in an exam, number nodes in the order they are visited. It shows the examiner you understand DFS order and pruning at a glance.
lessons.task: Draw a 5 x 5 grid and solve 5-queens by hand with backtracking, writing each placement and each backtrack. Then try to colour a map of 6 neighbouring districts of your division with 3 colours using the same method.

quiz.q: What does backtracking do when a partial solution violates a constraint?
options: Undoes the last choice and tries the next option
quiz.explain: It prunes that branch and returns to the previous decision.

quiz.q: How many solutions does the 8-queens problem have?
quiz.explain: There are 92 solutions, 12 of them distinct up to symmetry.

quiz.q: In branch and bound for 0/1 knapsack, which upper bound is commonly used?
options: Current value plus the fractional knapsack value of the remaining items
quiz.explain: Allowing fractions gives an optimistic bound that is quick to compute.

quiz.q: For subset sum with {3, 5, 6, 7} and T = 15, which subset is found?
Which statement about backtracking is true?
options: It always runs in polynomial time
It is still exponential in the worst case but prunes many branches in practice
It never needs to undo choices
quiz.explain: Pruning helps a lot, but NP-hard problems remain hard in the worst case.

lessons.title: String Matching: Naive, Rabin-Karp, KMP
lessons.content:
Imagine pressing Ctrl+F in a long PDF of the Bangladesh constitution and typing 'citizen'. In a blink, every occurrence is highlighted. Behind that blink is a string matching algorithm. The simple way would compare the word at every position, which is fine for a page but slow for a whole library or a DNA sequence with billions of letters. In this lesson we study the naive method, the Rabin-Karp rolling hash, and the Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) algorithm with its prefix function, and compare their running times.

The problem: We have a text T of length n and a pattern P of length m, with m <= n, over some alphabet, such as English letters, Bangla letters, digits or the DNA letters A, C, G, T. We want every shift s, from 0 to n - m, such that T[s+1 .. s+m] = P[1 .. m]. Each such s is a valid shift, or an occurrence of P in T.

The naive algorithm: For every shift s from 0 to n - m, compare P with the text window starting at s, character by character, and stop at the first mismatch. In code: for s from 0 to n - m: j = 0; while j < m and T[s + j] == P[j]: j = j + 1; if j == m: report s. Simple and correct.

Naive, the analysis: There are n - m + 1 shifts and each can take up to m comparisons, so the worst case is O((n - m + 1) m), which is O(nm). The bad case: T = AAAA...A (n letters) and P = AAA...AB (m letters). At every shift, m - 1 characters match before the B fails. On random English text, mismatches usually come quickly and the naive method is fast in practice, but we want a guarantee.

The waste in the naive method: When a window fails after matching many characters, the naive method moves one step and forgets everything it learned. If P = ABABC and we matched ABAB before failing, we already know the text there is ABAB. Both KMP and Rabin-Karp avoid this waste, in very different ways: Rabin-Karp turns comparison into cheap arithmetic, while KMP remembers what has been matched.

Rabin-Karp, the idea: Treat each m-character string as a number, compute a hash of the pattern, and compare it with the hash of each text window. If hashes differ, the strings certainly differ. If hashes match, check the characters to be sure. The trick that makes it fast is a rolling hash: the hash of the next window is computed from the previous one in O(1) time.

The rolling hash: With digits as the alphabet and base d = 10, a window like 314 is the number 314. Sliding to the next window, 141, means: remove the leading digit's contribution, shift left, and add the new digit: 141 = (314 - 3 times 100) times 10 + 1. To keep numbers small, do everything modulo a prime q: t_(s+1) = (d (t_s - T[s+1] h) + T[s+m+1]) mod q, where h = d^(m-1) mod q. For letters, use d = alphabet size, like 256.

Rabin-Karp worked example: Text 3141592653589, pattern 26, q = 11. Hash of the pattern: 26 mod 11 = 4. Window hashes: 31 gives 9, 14 gives 3, 41 gives 8, 15 gives 4, 59 gives 4, 92 gives 4, 26 gives 4, 65 gives 10, and so on. Hash matches occur at windows 15, 59, 92 and 26. Character checks reject 15, 59 and 92; these are spurious hits. Only 26, at shift 6, is a real match. Rolling check: from 31 (hash 9) to 14: ((9 - 3 times 10) times 10 + 4) mod 11 = (-206) mod 11 = 3. Correct.

Rabin-Karp, the analysis: Preprocessing the pattern hash and h is O(m). Each window hash is O(1) by rolling, so scanning is O(n) plus the cost of character checks. With a good large prime, spurious hits are rare, and the expected time is O(n + m). In the worst case, if every window is a hash hit (for example many true matches or a bad q), each check costs O(m), giving O(nm). Choosing q as a large random prime makes bad cases very unlikely.

Where Rabin-Karp shines: It extends easily to searching for many patterns at once: put all pattern hashes in a hash set, and check each window's hash against the set. Plagiarism detectors use this idea, hashing every k-word chunk of a document and looking for chunks shared with other documents. It also extends to two-dimensional pattern search in images.

KMP, the idea: Knuth, Morris and Pratt (1977) found a way to never move backwards in the text. When a mismatch happens after matching q characters of P, the algorithm already knows those q text characters, because they equal P[1..q]. So it can compute, from the pattern alone, how far the pattern can safely slide. This information is stored in the prefix function.

The prefix function: For each position q of the pattern, pi[q] is the length of the longest proper prefix of P[1..q] that is also a suffix of P[1..q]. Proper means not the whole string. Example: P = ABABACA. For q = 5, P[1..5] = ABABA; the prefix ABA is also a suffix, and no longer proper prefix works, so pi[5] = 3. The full table is pi = [0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1].

Computing the prefix function: k = 0; pi[1] = 0. For q from 2 to m: while k > 0 and P[k+1] != P[q]: k = pi[k]. If P[k+1] == P[q]: k = k + 1. pi[q] = k. The while loop falls back through shorter borders. Although it looks like it could be slow, an amortized argument (lesson 11) shows the total work is O(m): k increases at most m times, and each fall back decreases it, so it cannot decrease more than it increased.

The KMP matcher: q = 0 (number of characters matched). For i from 1 to n: while q > 0 and P[q+1] != T[i]: q = pi[q]. If P[q+1] == T[i]: q = q + 1. If q == m: report a match at shift i - m; q = pi[q] to keep looking for overlapping matches. The text index i only moves forward. By the same amortized argument, the matcher is O(n), so KMP is O(n + m) in the worst case, not just on average.

KMP worked example: Text ABABABACA, pattern ABABACA, pi = [0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1]. Match A, B, A, B, A: q = 5. Next text char is B, but P[6] = C, mismatch. Fall back q = pi[5] = 3, meaning ABA is still matched. P[4] = B matches the text B: q = 4. Then A: q = 5. C: q = 6. A: q = 7 = m, match found at shift 2. The naive method would have restarted at shift 1 and re-read characters; KMP never re-reads the text.

Another prefix function to practise: For P = AABAAB, pi = [0, 1, 0, 1, 2, 3]. For P = ABABCABAB, pi = [0, 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4]. Check one: for q = 9, ABABCABAB, the prefix ABAB equals the suffix ABAB, length 4. Being fluent with this table is the key to every KMP exam question.

The finite automaton view: CLRS also presents a string matching automaton. For a pattern of length m, build a machine with states 0 to m, where state q means 'the last q text characters match the first q pattern characters'. For each state and each alphabet letter, precompute the next state. Then the text is scanned with exactly one table lookup per character, O(n) matching time. The catch is preprocessing: the table has (m + 1) times the alphabet size entries, which is expensive for large alphabets like Unicode. KMP can be seen as a clever way to get the same effect while storing only the m values of pi and computing transitions on the fly.

Comparison of the three: Naive: no preprocessing, O(nm) worst case, simple and fine for short patterns. Rabin-Karp: O(m) preprocessing, O(n + m) expected and O(nm) worst case, great for multiple patterns. KMP: O(m) preprocessing, O(n + m) worst case, never backs up in the text, ideal for streaming data. In practice, tools like grep use variants such as Boyer-Moore, which skips ahead using the last characters of the pattern and is often sublinear on normal text.

Real life example 1, searching Bangla text: A Bangla news site lets readers search old articles for a phrase. Bangla text in Unicode uses several code points per visible letter, so patterns can be long in code units. KMP's guarantee of O(n + m) with no backtracking over the text is useful when articles are streamed from storage. Search engines, of course, build indexes in advance, but string matching is still used to highlight the matched phrase inside each result.

Real life example 2, DNA and virus detection: Researchers studying dengue or COVID-19 samples in Bangladesh search long genome sequences, strings over A, C, G, T, for known marker patterns. With a genome of 30,000 letters and hundreds of markers, a Rabin-Karp style multi-pattern search or its relative, the Aho-Corasick automaton, finds all markers in one pass. Antivirus programs use the same idea to scan files for many virus signatures at once.

Common mistakes: First, in Rabin-Karp, forgetting to verify characters on a hash match, which reports spurious hits as real matches. Second, getting a negative number after subtraction in the rolling formula; add q before taking mod. Third, in the prefix function, including the whole string as a prefix; it must be a proper prefix. Fourth, after a full KMP match, resetting q to 0 instead of pi[m], which misses overlapping matches like finding AA in AAAA.

What exams ask: 'Compute the prefix function for ABABACA.' 'Run KMP on this text and pattern, showing q after each character.' 'Show the Rabin-Karp hashes for this text with q = 11 or 13, and point out spurious hits.' 'Give the worst case of the naive algorithm and an input that causes it.' 'Compare the three algorithms.' A small table with columns i, T[i], q is the clearest way to show KMP.

Recap: String matching finds all shifts where P occurs in T. Naive checks every shift, O(nm) worst case. Rabin-Karp compares rolling hashes mod a prime and verifies on hits, O(n + m) expected, O(nm) worst. KMP precomputes the prefix function pi in O(m) and scans the text once without backing up, O(n + m) worst case, thanks to an amortized argument. Next: P, NP and NP-completeness, where we ask which problems have fast algorithms at all.
key_points: String matching finds every shift s where pattern P (length m) occurs in text T (length n).
Naive: check every shift; O(nm) worst case, e.g. T = AAAA...A, P = AA...AB.
Rabin-Karp: rolling hash mod a prime q; verify characters on hash hits; O(n + m) expected, O(nm) worst.
Rolling update: t_(s+1) = (d (t_s - T[s+1] h) + T[s+m+1]) mod q with h = d^(m-1) mod q.
Prefix function pi[q] = longest proper prefix of P[1..q] that is also its suffix; computed in O(m).
KMP never moves back in the text: O(n + m) worst case; after a match set q = pi[m].
Rabin-Karp suits many patterns at once; KMP suits streaming; Boyer-Moore is often fastest in practice.
lessons.tip: Practise the prefix function on five different patterns until you can write it in under a minute. Almost every KMP question starts with that table.
lessons.task: Write the prefix function for your own name in capital English letters (for example ANANYA or RAHIM). Then write a 20-letter text containing your name twice and run KMP by hand, recording q after each letter.

quiz.q: In Rabin-Karp, what is a spurious hit?
options: A window whose hash equals the pattern's hash but whose characters differ
A pattern longer than the text
quiz.explain: Equal hashes do not guarantee equal strings; characters must be checked.

quiz.q: What is the prefix function of ABABACA?
quiz.explain: For example pi[5] = 3 because ABA is both a prefix and a suffix of ABABA.

quiz.q: What is the worst-case time of KMP?
quiz.explain: Prefix function O(m) and matcher O(n) by an amortized argument.

quiz.explain: Resetting to pi[m] keeps the longest border so overlapping occurrences are found.

lessons.title: P, NP and NP-Completeness
lessons.content:
Imagine your friend gives you a finished Sudoku and asks, 'Is this correct?' You check every row, column and box in a minute. Now imagine she gives you an empty, very large Sudoku and asks you to solve it. That can take hours, or for giant puzzles, longer than a lifetime. Checking an answer is easy; finding one seems hard. This gap between checking and finding is the heart of the most famous open question in computer science: is P equal to NP? In this lesson we learn what P and NP mean, what reductions are, why SAT is special, the classic NP-complete problems, and what NP-hard means.

Tractable and intractable: So far, almost every algorithm in this course ran in polynomial time: O(n), O(n log n), O(n^3). We call problems with polynomial-time algorithms tractable. For some problems, like 0/1 knapsack with large weights, travelling salesman and graph colouring, we only know exponential algorithms. With n = 100, an algorithm needing 2^n steps would run far longer than the age of the universe, even on a computer doing a billion steps per second: about 40 trillion years. Such problems are called intractable in practice.

Decision problems: To build a clean theory, we mostly study decision problems, whose answer is yes or no. Instead of 'find the shortest tour', ask 'is there a tour of length at most k?'. Instead of 'colour this graph with the fewest colours', ask 'can it be coloured with 3 colours?'. This is not a big loss: if we can answer the decision version quickly, we can usually find the optimal value by binary search on k, and often the solution itself.

The class P: P is the set of decision problems that can be solved by an algorithm in polynomial time, O(n^c) for some constant c, where n is the input size in bits. Examples: is there a path from s to t? (BFS). Is this array sorted? Is the shortest path from s to t at most k? (Dijkstra). Does this graph have a perfect matching? (max flow). Is this number prime? (yes, the AKS algorithm, 2002, put primality in P).

The class NP: NP is the set of decision problems where, whenever the answer is yes, there is a short proof, called a certificate, that can be checked in polynomial time. For 'is there a tour of length at most k?', the certificate is the tour itself; checking it means verifying it visits every city once and adding up its length. For 'can this graph be 3-coloured?', the certificate is the colouring; checking means looking at every edge. NP stands for nondeterministic polynomial time, not 'not polynomial'.

P is inside NP: Every problem in P is also in NP. If you can solve it in polynomial time, you can verify a yes answer by simply solving it again, ignoring the certificate. So P is a subset of NP. The big open question is whether NP contains problems that are not in P. Most researchers believe P is not equal to NP, but nobody has proved it. The Clay Mathematics Institute offers one million US dollars for a proof either way.

Why P versus NP matters: If P = NP, then every problem whose solution can be checked quickly could also be solved quickly. Many cryptographic systems used for online banking, such as RSA, rely on certain problems being hard to solve but easy to check. Proving P = NP with a practical algorithm would change cryptography, scheduling, logistics and more. Proving P is not NP would confirm that some problems are inherently hard.

Reductions: A reduction transforms one problem into another. We say A reduces to B in polynomial time, written A <=p B, if there is a polynomial-time function f that turns any instance x of A into an instance f(x) of B, such that x is a yes instance of A exactly when f(x) is a yes instance of B. Then, if B can be solved quickly, so can A: transform and solve. In words, A is no harder than B.

A simple reduction example: Bipartite matching reduces to max flow, as in lesson 22: build the flow network from the bipartite graph; a matching of size k exists if and only if the max flow is at least k. Another: Hamiltonian cycle reduces to TSP: given a graph, make a complete graph where original edges cost 1 and missing edges cost 2; there is a Hamiltonian cycle if and only if there is a tour of cost exactly n.

NP-hard and NP-complete: A problem B is NP-hard if every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time. It is at least as hard as anything in NP. A problem is NP-complete if it is NP-hard and also in NP. NP-complete problems are the hardest problems in NP. If any single NP-complete problem had a polynomial algorithm, then every NP problem would, and P would equal NP.

The first NP-complete problem, SAT: The satisfiability problem SAT asks: given a Boolean formula with variables x1, x2, ... and operators AND, OR, NOT, is there an assignment of true and false that makes the whole formula true? Example: (x1 OR NOT x2) AND (x2 OR x3) AND (NOT x1 OR NOT x3). Try x1 = true, x2 = true, x3 = false: first clause true, second true, third true. Satisfiable.

Cook-Levin theorem: In 1971, Stephen Cook, and independently Leonid Levin, proved that SAT is NP-complete. The idea: any NP problem has a polynomial-time verifier, which is a machine running for polynomially many steps. One can write a large but polynomial-size Boolean formula that is satisfiable exactly when some certificate makes the verifier accept. This was the seed. After that, proving a new problem NP-complete only needs a reduction from a known NP-complete problem.

3-SAT: 3-SAT restricts SAT to formulas in conjunctive normal form with exactly three literals per clause. It is still NP-complete, and it is the favourite starting point for reductions because its structure is simple. Interestingly, 2-SAT, with two literals per clause, is in P and can be solved in linear time with strongly connected components, the Kosaraju idea from lesson 18.

The recipe for proving NP-completeness: To prove a new problem X is NP-complete: Step 1, show X is in NP by describing a certificate and a polynomial-time verifier. Step 2, pick a known NP-complete problem Y. Step 3, give a polynomial-time reduction from Y to X: transform any instance of Y into an instance of X. Step 4, prove both directions: yes for Y implies yes for X, and yes for X implies yes for Y. Direction matters: reduce from the known hard problem to the new one, never the other way.

Classic NP-complete problems: Richard Karp showed in 1972 that 21 natural problems are NP-complete. The most commonly taught: SAT and 3-SAT; CLIQUE (does the graph have k vertices all connected to each other?); INDEPENDENT SET (k vertices with no edges between them); VERTEX COVER (k vertices touching every edge); HAMILTONIAN CYCLE (a cycle visiting every vertex once); TSP decision version; SUBSET SUM; 0/1 KNAPSACK decision version; GRAPH 3-COLOURING; and SET COVER.

A neat chain of reductions: 3-SAT reduces to CLIQUE: for each clause make a group of three vertices for its literals, connect vertices from different groups unless they are contradictory, like x and NOT x; the formula is satisfiable if and only if there is a clique of size equal to the number of clauses. CLIQUE reduces to INDEPENDENT SET by taking the complement graph. INDEPENDENT SET of size k exists if and only if VERTEX COVER of size n - k exists, since the vertices outside an independent set cover every edge.

NP-hard beyond NP: Some problems are NP-hard but not in NP, usually because they are not decision problems or their yes answers have no short certificate. The optimisation version of TSP, 'find the shortest tour', is NP-hard. The halting problem is NP-hard too, and it is not even solvable at all. So NP-hard means 'at least as hard as NP', with no upper limit.

What to do with an NP-hard problem: Do not give up; change the question. Use exact exponential methods for small inputs, like backtracking or branch and bound (lesson 23) or DP with pseudo-polynomial time (lesson 15). Use approximation algorithms with a guaranteed ratio (lesson 26). Use heuristics like local search or genetic algorithms that work well in practice without guarantees. Or look for special cases in P, such as TSP on very small graphs, knapsack with small capacity, or 2-SAT.

Real life example 1, the exam routine problem: A university with 500 courses wants an exam routine in 10 days with no student having two exams on one day. This is graph colouring, NP-complete in general. The exam office does not need a perfect theory; it uses heuristics like 'schedule the most conflicting course first' and accepts a good routine. Knowing the problem is NP-complete saves the IT team from searching forever for a fast exact algorithm that probably does not exist.

Real life example 2, delivery routing: Daraz, Foodpanda and courier companies plan routes for thousands of deliveries daily. Their core problem is a version of TSP and vehicle routing, both NP-hard. They use approximation and smart heuristics, combined with exact solvers for small parts of the problem. The theory of NP-completeness tells engineers which parts are fundamentally hard and where to focus clever tricks.

Common mistakes: First, thinking NP means 'not polynomial'; it means nondeterministic polynomial, and P is inside NP. Second, reducing in the wrong direction: to show X is hard, reduce a known hard problem to X. Third, forgetting to show the problem is in NP when proving NP-completeness. Fourth, saying NP-complete problems can never be solved; they can, just not known to be solvable in polynomial time. Fifth, calling knapsack's O(nW) a polynomial algorithm, which would wrongly imply P = NP.

What exams ask: 'Define P, NP, NP-hard and NP-complete with examples.' 'Draw the relationship between P, NP, NP-complete and NP-hard assuming P is not NP.' 'State the Cook-Levin theorem.' 'Show that vertex cover is in NP.' 'Reduce independent set to vertex cover.' 'Why does a polynomial algorithm for one NP-complete problem imply P = NP?' A clear Venn diagram and a careful statement of reduction direction earn most marks.

The picture to remember: Assuming P is not NP, draw a big oval NP. Inside it, a smaller region P on one side. On the other edge of NP, the NP-complete problems. A larger region NP-hard overlaps NP exactly at NP-complete and extends outside NP. If P = NP, the picture collapses: P, NP and NP-complete become the same set, apart from trivial problems.

Recap: P contains decision problems solvable in polynomial time; NP contains those whose yes answers can be verified in polynomial time with a certificate; P is a subset of NP, and whether they are equal is open. A reduction A <=p B shows A is no harder than B. NP-hard means every NP problem reduces to it; NP-complete means NP-hard and in NP. SAT was the first NP-complete problem (Cook-Levin), followed by 3-SAT, CLIQUE, vertex cover, Hamiltonian cycle, TSP, subset sum, knapsack and 3-colouring. Next: approximation and randomized algorithms, and a wrap-up of the course.
key_points: P = decision problems solvable in polynomial time; NP = those whose yes answers have certificates verifiable in polynomial time.
P is a subset of NP; whether P = NP is the biggest open question in computer science.
A reduction A <=p B transforms instances in polynomial time preserving yes/no, so A is no harder than B.
NP-hard: every NP problem reduces to it. NP-complete: NP-hard and in NP.
Cook-Levin (1971): SAT is NP-complete; 3-SAT, CLIQUE, vertex cover, Hamiltonian cycle, TSP, subset sum, knapsack and 3-colouring followed.
To prove X NP-complete: show X in NP, then reduce a known NP-complete problem to X, both directions.
For NP-hard problems use small exact search, pseudo-polynomial DP, approximation, heuristics or special cases.
lessons.tip: Whenever you write a reduction, first write one line: 'from KNOWN-HARD to NEW'. Checking that line before anything else prevents the most common mark-losing mistake.
lessons.task: Write a small 3-SAT formula with 3 variables and 3 clauses. Find a satisfying assignment by trying cases, and count how many of the 8 assignments you had to try. Then think: how many would 30 variables need?

Reduce a known NP-complete problem to X
Write a fast algorithm for X

P is a subset of NP

lessons.title: Approximation and Randomized Algorithms, and Course Wrap-up
lessons.content:
Imagine a cricket coach who has ten minutes to pick a batting order. The perfect order might take days to compute, but he knows a simple rule that is never worse than twice the ideal. He uses it and wins the match. Or imagine a teacher who checks a huge pile of homework by picking a random sample of pages instead of reading everything. Both are wise trade-offs: good enough answers fast, or correct answers with a little help from luck. This final lesson covers approximation algorithms, randomized algorithms, and then wraps up the whole course with a cheat-sheet of paradigms and what to learn next.

Why approximation: Lesson 25 showed that many important optimisation problems are NP-hard, so we probably cannot solve them exactly in polynomial time. An approximation algorithm runs in polynomial time and returns a solution that is provably close to optimal. Not a guess, a guarantee.

The approximation ratio: For a minimisation problem, an algorithm has ratio rho if, for every input, its cost C satisfies C <= rho times C*, where C* is the optimal cost. For maximisation, C >= C* / rho. A 2-approximation for a minimisation problem never returns more than twice the optimal cost. The proof usually compares the algorithm's answer with a lower bound on C*, because C* itself is unknown.

Vertex cover, the problem: In a graph, a vertex cover is a set of vertices touching every edge. Finding the smallest one is NP-hard. Think of placing security guards at corridor junctions so that every corridor is watched from at least one end.

Vertex cover, the 2-approximation: C = empty. While there are uncovered edges: pick any uncovered edge (u, v), add both u and v to C, and remove all edges touching u or v. Return C. Time O(V + E). Simple, almost silly, and yet provably good.

Why it is a 2-approximation: Let A be the set of edges the algorithm picked. No two edges in A share a vertex, because after picking (u, v) we remove all edges touching them. So A is a matching. Any vertex cover, including the optimal one, must contain at least one endpoint of each edge in A, and since these edges are disjoint, different edges need different vertices. So C* >= |A|. The algorithm adds 2 vertices per edge: |C| = 2|A| <= 2 C*. The lower bound used is the size of a matching.

Vertex cover example: A path a, b, c, d, e with edges a-b, b-c, c-d, d-e. Optimal cover: {b, d}, size 2. The algorithm might pick edge b-c, add b and c, removing a-b, b-c and c-d; then pick d-e, add d and e. Cover {b, c, d, e}, size 4, exactly 2 times the optimum, matching the bound. A natural greedy idea, 'pick the vertex with the highest degree', sounds smarter but has no constant ratio; its worst case grows like log n.

Metric TSP, the setting: In TSP with the triangle inequality, the direct road is never longer than a detour: w(a, c) <= w(a, b) + w(b, c). Real road distances roughly satisfy this. General TSP cannot be approximated within any constant unless P = NP, but metric TSP can.

Metric TSP, the 2-approximation idea: Step 1, compute a minimum spanning tree T (lesson 19). Step 2, walk around the tree, a full DFS walk that goes down and back up every edge, which costs exactly 2 w(T). Step 3, shortcut: list cities in the order they are first visited in the walk, skipping repeats, and return to the start. Shortcuts never increase length because of the triangle inequality.

Why it is within 2: Removing any one edge from an optimal tour leaves a spanning path, which is a spanning tree, so w(T) <= C*. The full walk costs 2 w(T) <= 2 C*, and shortcutting only makes it shorter. So the tour is at most twice the optimum. Christofides' algorithm improves the ratio to 1.5 by adding a minimum-weight perfect matching on the odd-degree vertices of T. For exams, the MST-based 2-approximation is the standard one to explain.

Metric TSP worked example: Four towns A, B, C, D on a straight road at kilometre marks 0, 1, 2 and 3, so distances are just differences. An MST is the chain A-B, B-C, C-D with weight 3. The full walk from A is A, B, C, D, C, B, A with length 6. Shortcutting repeated towns gives the tour A, B, C, D, A with length 1 + 1 + 1 + 3 = 6. The optimal tour also has length 6, since any tour must go out to D and come back. Here the approximation happens to be optimal; the guarantee only promises at most twice the optimum, and on other inputs the gap can be larger.

Other approximation ideas briefly: Greedy set cover achieves ratio about ln n. Knapsack has a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS): for any epsilon, a solution within (1 - epsilon) of optimal in time polynomial in n and 1/epsilon, by rounding values and using DP. These show that NP-hard problems differ a lot in how well they can be approximated.

Randomized algorithms: A randomized algorithm makes random choices during its run, like flipping coins. The randomness is in the algorithm, not in the input, so the guarantees hold for every input. We already met randomized quick sort (lesson 7), randomized select (lesson 10) and Rabin-Karp with a random prime (lesson 24).

Las Vegas algorithms: A Las Vegas algorithm always gives the correct answer, but its running time is random. Randomized quick sort is the classic example: the output is always sorted, and the expected time is O(n log n), although an unlucky run could take O(n^2). Quickselect is another. You can think: 'the result is guaranteed, the time is a gamble with very good odds'.

Monte Carlo algorithms: A Monte Carlo algorithm always runs within a fixed time bound, but its answer may be wrong with some small probability. Example: the Miller-Rabin primality test. For a number n, pick a random base and do a quick check. If n is prime, it always says 'probably prime'. If n is composite, each round wrongly says 'probably prime' with probability at most 1/4. After 20 independent rounds, the error probability is at most (1/4)^20, less than one in a trillion. Cryptography libraries use this to find large primes for RSA.

Another Monte Carlo example, Freivalds' check: Given three n by n matrices A, B and C, is AB = C? Computing AB costs O(n^3). Freivalds picks a random 0/1 vector r and checks whether A(Br) = Cr, which needs only three matrix-vector products, O(n^2). If AB = C, the test always passes. If not, it fails with probability at least 1/2. Repeat k times to make the error at most 1/2^k. Fast checking of a slow computation.

Karger's randomized min cut: Another famous Monte Carlo algorithm finds a minimum cut of an undirected graph by repeatedly picking a random edge and contracting it, merging its two endpoints, until only two super-vertices remain. The edges between them form a cut. A single run finds a minimum cut with probability at least 2/(n(n - 1)), which is small, but repeating it about n^2 log n times makes failure very unlikely. It is a beautiful example of how a very simple random process can solve a non-trivial graph problem.

Las Vegas versus Monte Carlo: Las Vegas: correct always, time random. Monte Carlo: time fixed, correctness probabilistic. You can turn Las Vegas into Monte Carlo by stopping after a time limit and giving up or guessing. You can turn Monte Carlo into Las Vegas if you can quickly verify an answer: repeat until the verifier accepts. A memory trick: Las Vegas casinos never let you leave with the wrong amount of money, but you do not know how long you will stay.

Course cheat-sheet, analysis tools: Asymptotic notation O, Omega, Theta (lesson 2). Loop counting and invariants (lesson 3). Recurrences by substitution, unrolling, recursion trees and the master theorem (lessons 4 and 5). Amortized analysis by aggregate, accounting and potential (lesson 11). Lower bounds by decision trees (lesson 9). Reductions and NP-completeness (lesson 25).

Course cheat-sheet, design paradigms: Divide and conquer: split, solve, combine; merge sort, quick sort, Karatsuba, Strassen, closest pair. Greedy: one safe local choice, proved by exchange; activity selection, Huffman, Kruskal, Prim, Dijkstra. Dynamic programming: overlapping subproblems in a table; knapsack, LCS, edit distance, matrix chain, Floyd-Warshall, Bellman-Ford. Graph search: BFS, DFS, topological sort, SCC, max flow. Backtracking and branch and bound for exact search. Approximation and randomization for hard or huge problems.

Choosing a paradigm, a quick guide: If the problem splits into independent parts, try divide and conquer. If a simple rule seems to work and you can prove it with an exchange argument, use greedy. If brute force repeats the same subproblems, use DP. If it is about connections, model it as a graph. If it looks NP-hard, consider backtracking for small inputs and approximation or heuristics for large ones. Always start with a correct brute force and improve it.

Real life example 1, placing CCTV cameras: A city corporation wants cameras at intersections so that every street is watched. This is vertex cover. With thousands of intersections, an exact solution is too slow, but the 2-approximation runs in milliseconds and guarantees no more than twice the minimum number of cameras. Engineers then improve it locally, removing cameras that are not needed.

Real life example 2, secure messaging: When you set up a secure chat or log in to online banking, the server and your phone may need large random primes, for example to create RSA keys. They use the Miller-Rabin Monte Carlo test, repeated enough times that an error is less likely than a hardware fault. Randomization makes this fast and practically certain.

What to learn next: After this course, good next steps are Theory of Computation (automata, computability, complexity in depth), Advanced Algorithms (randomized and approximation algorithms, network flows, linear programming), Computational Geometry, and Machine Learning, which relies heavily on optimisation. For practice, solve problems on online judges like Codeforces, LeetCode or the Bangladeshi platform Toph, and take part in ICPC-style contests, where Bangladeshi university teams have a strong tradition.

Common mistakes and exam focus: Confusing approximation ratio direction for minimisation and maximisation; forgetting to state the lower bound in a ratio proof; mixing up Las Vegas and Monte Carlo; claiming randomized quick sort is Monte Carlo. Exams ask: 'Give a 2-approximation for vertex cover and prove the ratio.' 'Explain the MST-based approximation for metric TSP.' 'Differentiate Las Vegas and Monte Carlo with examples.' 'Which paradigm would you use for this problem and why?'

Recap: Approximation algorithms give provable closeness to optimal in polynomial time: vertex cover via a maximal matching is a 2-approximation; metric TSP via MST walk and shortcuts is a 2-approximation. Randomized algorithms use coin flips: Las Vegas is always correct with random time (randomized quick sort), Monte Carlo has fixed time with small error (Miller-Rabin, Freivalds). Across the course you learned to analyse algorithms and to design them with divide and conquer, greedy, DP, graph methods, search and approximation. Congratulations on finishing Algorithms.
key_points: An approximation algorithm runs in polynomial time with a proven ratio: C <= rho C* for minimisation.
Vertex cover 2-approximation: repeatedly take both ends of an uncovered edge; picked edges form a matching, so C* >= |A|.
Metric TSP 2-approximation: MST, full walk (2 w(T)), shortcut; w(T) <= C*. Christofides achieves 1.5.
Las Vegas: always correct, random time (randomized quick sort, quickselect).
Monte Carlo: fixed time, small error probability (Miller-Rabin, Freivalds); repeat to shrink error.
Paradigms: divide and conquer, greedy, DP, graph search, backtracking/branch and bound, approximation, randomization.
Next: Theory of Computation, Advanced Algorithms, and regular practice on online judges and contests.
lessons.tip: Make your own one-page cheat-sheet of every algorithm in this course with its paradigm, recurrence or key idea, and running time. Writing it yourself is the best revision before the final exam.
lessons.task: Draw a small map of 6 to 8 intersections near your home with streets as edges. Run the 2-approximation vertex cover by hand to place 'cameras', then try to find the true minimum by inspection and compare the two sizes.

quiz.q: The edge-picking vertex cover algorithm has approximation ratio
quiz.explain: Picked edges form a matching, which lower-bounds the optimum; we take 2 vertices per edge.

quiz.q: The MST-based metric TSP approximation relies on which property?
quiz.explain: Shortcuts never increase length when w(a, c) <= w(a, b) + w(b, c).

quiz.q: Randomized quick sort is an example of a
quiz.explain: It is always correct; only its running time is random.

quiz.q: After 20 independent Miller-Rabin rounds on a composite number, the error probability is at most
quiz.explain: Each round errs with probability at most 1/4, independently.

quiz.q: Which paradigm fits best when brute force solves the same subproblems again and again?
quiz.explain: DP stores each overlapping subproblem's answer once.

lessons.title: What Computer Architecture and Organization Are
lessons.content:
Imagine you open the back of an old desktop computer at a repair shop in Dhaka's IDB Bhaban. You see a green board, a chip with a fan on top, some long sticks of RAM, and a lot of tiny lines running between them. You type a message on Facebook, and somehow these silent pieces of metal and silicon turn your key presses into letters on the screen, send them across the world, and show a reply. How? That question, 'how does the machine actually do it inside?', is what this whole course is about.

What it is in one line: Computer Architecture and Organization is the study of how a computer is designed and built so that it can run programs. It explains what the processor understands, how it is put together from smaller parts, how it talks to memory and to input and output devices, and how designers make it fast, cheap and low on power.

The problem it solves: Software people write programs in languages like C, Python or Dart. Hardware people build circuits from transistors and logic gates. These two worlds speak completely different languages. A transistor knows nothing about a 'for loop', and a Python programmer does not want to think about voltages. Somebody has to design the bridge between them: a clear agreement about what the hardware will do when the software asks for something, and a smart way to build hardware that keeps that promise quickly. That bridge is computer architecture.

Before this idea was clear: The earliest electronic computers of the 1940s, like ENIAC, were 'programmed' by plugging cables and setting switches by hand. Changing the program could take days. Every new machine also had its own completely different set of commands, so a program written for one machine was useless on the next one. In 1964 IBM launched the System/360 family and made a big decision: several machines with very different speeds and prices would all understand the same set of instructions. A customer could buy a small model, write programs, and later move to a bigger model without rewriting anything. That was the moment people clearly separated 'what the machine promises' from 'how a particular machine is built'. Those two halves are exactly the two words in our course title.

Architecture, the promise: Computer architecture is the part of the design that a programmer (or a compiler) can see. It answers questions like: What instructions exist, such as ADD, LOAD, STORE, JUMP? How many registers are there and how big is each one? How are numbers stored, for example 32-bit two's complement integers? How does an instruction say where its data is? What happens when something goes wrong, like dividing by zero? The official name for this list of promises is the Instruction Set Architecture, or ISA. x86-64 (used in most Intel and AMD laptops) and ARM (used in almost all smartphones) are two famous ISAs.

Organization, the building: Computer organization is how a specific chip actually keeps those promises. It answers questions like: How many adders are inside the ALU? Is there a cache, and how big? Is the processor pipelined, and how many stages? How wide is the bus to memory? Is multiplication done in one clock tick or ten? A programmer usually cannot see these details directly; she only notices that one chip runs her program faster than another. Two processors can have the same architecture but very different organization.

A restaurant analogy: Think of a restaurant in Old Dhaka famous for kacchi biryani. The menu is the architecture: it tells customers exactly what they can order and what they will get. 'One plate kacchi, one borhani' is like an instruction. The kitchen is the organization: how many cooks, how many big handis, whether one cook does everything or there is an assembly line where one person cuts, one cooks, one serves. Two branches of the same restaurant can share the same menu (same architecture) but have very different kitchens (different organization). A small branch in Mirpur has one cook; the main branch has ten cooks working in parallel. The customer gets the same biryani from both, only faster at one.

Where the analogy breaks: In a restaurant, a customer can often peek into the kitchen and sometimes even ask for changes. In a computer, the line between architecture and organization is strict: software must work correctly no matter how the inside is organized. Also, a real processor follows instructions with total obedience and zero creativity; a cook might 'improve' your order, a CPU never will. The analogy helps you remember the split, but the real rules are much stricter.

A real example of the split: Intel's Core i3 and Core i9 processors of the same generation both run the x86-64 instruction set. The same Windows and the same Chrome browser run on both. That is the shared architecture. But the i9 has more cores, a larger cache and often a higher clock speed. That is different organization. Similarly, a cheap Android phone and an expensive one both use the ARM architecture, so the same app from the Play Store works on both, yet one feels much faster because of how its chip is organized inside.

Levels of abstraction: Computer scientists handle complexity by stacking layers, where each layer only needs to understand the one directly below it. From top to bottom the stack looks like this: Application (your bKash app) -> High-level language (Kotlin, C) -> Compiler and operating system -> ISA (the architecture) -> Microarchitecture (the organization: datapath, control, pipeline, cache) -> Logic gates and flip-flops -> Transistors -> Physics of electrons. Each arrow means 'is built on top of'. The ISA sits right in the middle like a waist: everything above it is software, everything below it is hardware. This is why the ISA is often called the hardware/software interface.

Why the layers help: Because of this layering, a Bangladeshi app developer can write one Flutter app without knowing which exact chip is inside each customer's phone. The compiler turns the code into ARM instructions, and every ARM chip promises to run those instructions correctly. In the other direction, a chip designer at ARM or Apple can invent a faster cache without breaking any existing app, because the promise at the ISA level stays the same. Layers let thousands of people work on different parts without stepping on each other.

The main parts you will meet: Almost every computer has five classic parts. Input devices bring data in (keyboard, touch screen, microphone). Output devices send results out (display, speaker). Memory stores both programs and data. The datapath is the part of the processor that actually moves and transforms data: registers, the ALU and the connections between them. The control unit is the part that reads each instruction and tells the datapath what to do, step by step. Datapath plus control together form the processor, also called the CPU. Here is a simple picture: Input -> [ CPU = Control + Datapath ] <-> Memory, and CPU -> Output. You will study each of these boxes in depth in later lessons.
